title: Neomania
hook: The shiny replacement looks like progress until the old tool quietly keeps beating it under load.
counterintuition: Novelty feels like evidence of improvement, but newness mostly proves that something has not yet faced time; judge the upgrade by durability, maintenance, and tested use before calling it progress.
tryThisNow: Before buying or approving one new thing, write what the current version has survived and what proof the replacement has under real use.
keyTakeaway: Do not let newness borrow the reputation of progress. Make novelty pass a durability test first.

breakdown.fastRead: A safety team is shown a new drilling dashboard with smooth animations and a launch article taped beside it. The old checklist looks dull, but it has survived storms, tired crews, and broken radios. Neomania begins when the new thing gets credit before it has earned any. The fix is not to worship the past. Ask what the old system has survived, what the new system has proved, and what failure would cost during real use. New can win, but only after it beats durability.
breakdown.deepRead:
A new app lands on your phone with a clean icon and three features you did not know you needed. The old app is plain, slow to impress, and familiar enough to feel boring. That boredom is dangerous because it makes tested reliability look like lack of progress. You start comparing sparkle with silence. Sparkle gets your attention. Silence gets treated as absence.

Neomania is the pull toward the new because it is new. It flatters the part of the mind that wants to feel current, sharp, and early. A new tool can become a status signal before it becomes a working tool. A new method can make a team feel brave before it has done one hard shift. A new dashboard can make risk feel managed because risk now has prettier colors.

Newness is not proof.

The correction is a durability test. What has this old thing survived? What has the new thing survived? Who maintains it when the launch team leaves? What happens under delay, boredom, weather, fatigue, cheap parts, bad data, or ordinary human neglect? If the old method has passed those pressures and the new one has only passed a demo, the demo should not outrank the record.

This does not mean older is always better. Some old tools last because nobody had the power or budget to replace them. Some new tools solve real problems that older systems could never handle. The point is to compare survival records, not age. A new thing deserves adoption when it proves it can carry the actual load better than the durable thing it wants to replace.
breakdown.fullRead:
The orchestra panel hears a young violinist play with a tone that feels fresh after a long afternoon of careful, correct auditions. The voting sheet starts to tilt toward surprise. One judge says the choice would show courage. Another says the old criteria may be stale. Nobody has yet listened to the blind second excerpt where the same player rushes the quiet passage that the orchestra performs every winter. The new feeling is real. It is not enough.

Novelty is powerful because it arrives with a story already attached: this is the future, this is progress, this is what alert people notice before others do. Durability arrives with almost no story. It is the pipe that still holds pressure, the routine that still works at midnight, the fabric that still hangs correctly after fifty washes, the protocol that keeps its shape when the room is tired. It is easy to underrate because it is not asking to be admired.

Nassim Nicholas Taleb, in Antifragile, pressed on this point through the idea that survival time itself contains information. A technology, practice, or object that has lasted is not merely old; it has already passed through many filters that destroyed weaker rivals. That does not make it sacred. It makes it evidence. The new item may still be better, but it has less survival data. A durability test simply refuses to give the newcomer a trophy for having skipped the hard years.

What would this look like after three winters, not three demos?

A water district sees the problem in a permit folder. The new treatment system promises cleaner reporting, faster sensors, and a modern vendor portal. The old system looks clumsy on paper, but the maintenance crew can repair it in a storm, spare parts sit in town, and the failure modes are known. The decision should not be old versus new. It should be proved resilience versus claimed resilience. The new bid can win only by showing how it behaves when the ideal conditions disappear.

The counterweight matters because nostalgia can masquerade as wisdom. Some people use durability language to protect habit, status, or fear of learning. A brittle old system can survive only because everyone works around it quietly. A bad process can look durable because the harmed people have no seat in the room. The correction is not reverence for age. It is a demand that both sides show their record under pressure.

In practice, write two columns before the upgrade gets approved. In the first, list what the current method has survived: peak demand, training turnover, wet weather, bad data, impatient customers, repair delays, ordinary neglect. In the second, list what the new method has actually survived outside the sales deck. If the second column is thin, run a pilot in a harsh corner before replacing the whole system. If the second column is strong, move. Progress should be able to carry weight.

The best decisions make novelty earn trust without humiliating it. A pharmacy can test a new flu-shot layout for two busy Saturdays before moving every branch. A game studio can compare a new retention feature with boring long-term behavior, not first-week clicks. A fashion buyer can ask whether the new fabric holds shape after wear, not only whether the waitlist loves the photo. Neomania fades when the question changes from 'Is it new?' to 'What has it survived?'

examples.title: The dashboard in the safety huddle
examples.scenario: A press clipping about a new drilling dashboard lies beside the hard-hat signout board in the Aberdeen safety trailer. Helen, the safety supervisor, must decide between replacing the paper pressure checklist or running a storm-shift pilot first. She circles neomania on the clipping, asks what the dashboard has survived, and keeps the checklist live until the pilot handles a rough night.
examples.whatToDo: Make the new system prove itself under the same pressure the old one already survived.
examples.whyItMatters: New safety tools can look like progress before they have carried fatigue, weather, and crew habits.

examples.title: The audition vote that rewards surprise
examples.scenario: "That sounded alive," the guest conductor says while the voting sheet sits open on the orchestra table in Manchester. Geoff must decide between advancing the surprising violinist on first impression or replaying the blind technical excerpt. He marks novelty risk beside the score, asks for the second excerpt, and changes his vote only after the quiet passage holds.
examples.whatToDo: Separate freshness from performance under the work the role will actually require.
examples.whyItMatters: Novelty can make surprise feel like quality before the durable skill has been tested.

examples.title: The treatment system with the modern portal
examples.scenario: The permit folder smells of damp cardboard after the water district board carries it in from a rain-soaked truck. Isabelle must decide between recommending the new treatment system or requiring a harsh-condition pilot. She writes durability beside the maintenance page, shows the spare-parts gap to the engineer, and delays the bid until the vendor proves repair support.
examples.whatToDo: Ask how the new system behaves when normal local failure conditions arrive.
examples.whyItMatters: Durability lives in maintenance, parts, and known failure modes, not in launch claims.

examples.title: The feature that looks like progress
examples.scenario: You are staring at an inventory scan on a game studio retention board while first-week clicks flash green. Walter, the live-ops lead in Montreal, must decide between rolling out the new reward loop or comparing it with ninety-day player behavior. He writes progress risk on the scan, pauses the launch, and asks analytics to test whether players keep returning after the novelty fades.
examples.whatToDo: Test the new feature against durable behavior, not only early excitement.
examples.whyItMatters: Progress in a product means lasting use, not just a brief spike caused by freshness.

examples.title: The flu-shot layout with a clean new flow
examples.scenario: It took Janek one Saturday at the Krakow pharmacy counter to see why the elegant flu-shot layout failed. The pilot checklist looked cleaner than the old queue cards, but it broke when two parents arrived with forms and a refrigerator alarm sounded. As branch manager, he must decide whether to expand it. He writes Taleb beside the checklist and keeps the old cards until the layout survives two peak clinics.
examples.whatToDo: Let the new process face disorder before treating it as a replacement.
examples.whyItMatters: Taleb's durability pressure matters most when real use is messy, not when the process is demonstrated cleanly.

examples.title: The fabric waitlist that mistakes photos for wear
examples.scenario: Why did the waitlist love the fabric that came back stretched from the sample fitting? Yasmin pins a training still from the Milan showroom beside the return notes after the postmortem. She writes neomania across the still, shows the buyer how the old wool held shape after wear, and closes the preorder until the new fabric survives a wash-and-wear test.
examples.whatToDo: Make a fashionable new material pass the same use test as the boring reliable one.
examples.whyItMatters: Consumer excitement can reward novelty before the product proves durability in real bodies and real care.

reviewCards.front: A new tool looks like progress. What durability evidence should adoption require?
reviewCards.back: Ask what the old tool has survived and what the new one has proved under similar pressure. Launch energy is not durability.

reviewCards.front: A durable old process looks boring. What mistake threatens the decision?
reviewCards.back: Neomania can make tested reliability look stale. Boredom is not evidence that the old process has stopped working.

reviewCards.front: A vendor demo looks excellent. What missing evidence matters?
reviewCards.back: Ask how the tool performs with delays, bad data, weak training, repairs, and ordinary neglect.

reviewCards.front: Someone uses durability to block every change. What is the guardrail?
reviewCards.back: Durability is evidence, not a veto. A new option can win when it proves better survival under real conditions.

reviewCards.front: How do you compare old and new without nostalgia?
reviewCards.back: Use two survival records: what the old has handled, and what the new has handled outside the showroom.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Make novelty prove durability. Compare the old record and the new record under real pressure before treating replacement as progress.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a new tool impresses me, then I will list three pressures the old tool has survived before approving the replacement.
If a new process is proposed after a clean demo, then I will request a pilot under messy real conditions.
If early users love a new feature, then I will check repeat behavior after novelty fades before expanding it.
If I want the latest version, then I will compare maintenance, repair, and long-use evidence before buying.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one new thing you want. Write the old version's survival record, then find one real-use test the new version has passed or postpone the switch.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review one proposed upgrade and ask whether the new thing has proved progress or merely photographed well.

memorableLines.text: Progress should be able to carry weight.
Durability arrives with almost no story.
